item.title: Corticomuscular coupling alterations during task-dependent bimanual coordination after stroke: A multimodal functional near-infrared spectroscopy-surface electromyography analysis.
item.description:
Neural regeneration research
Abstract Post-stroke bimanual coordination dysfunction severely impairs activities of daily living. However, the underlying neurophysiological mechanisms remain incompletely understood, particularly regarding central-peripheral coupling characteristics under different bimanual coordination tasks and their distinction from aging effects. This study included 32 chronic subcortical stroke patients and 29 healthy controls. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy and surface electromyography signals were synchronously acquired during the execution of symmetrical and asymmetrical bimanual coordination tasks. Analyzed indices included cortical activation patterns, functional connectivity, corticomuscular coupling characterized by transfer entropy, intermuscular coupling, and muscle synergies. Correlations between these indices and the Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Upper Extremity and Modified Barthel Index were also evaluated. The results showed that during the symmetrical task, the ascending muscle-to-cortex connectivity was significantly reduced in the patient group, and this index was significantly positively correlated with the Modified Barthel Index. Brain functional connectivity and cortical activation were significantly increased in the patient group, and the connectivity from the ipsilesional prefrontal cortex to the contralesional SAC was significantly negatively correlated with Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Upper Extremity scores. Additionally, intermuscular coupling was significantly weakened, and muscle synergy patterns were abnormal in the patient group. During the asymmetrical task, no significant group differences in corticomuscular coupling were found, but brain functional connectivity and cortical activation were both significantly increased, and the connectivity from the ipsilesional supplementary motor area to the contralesional supplementary motor area was significantly positively correlated with MBI. Intermuscular coupling was significantly weakened, and muscle synergy patterns were abnormal. Attribution analysis suggested that cortical hyperactivation patterns and abnormal muscle synergies mainly reflect stroke effects, while abnormal sensory cortex activation and altered corticomuscular coupling may be influenced by both stroke and aging. This study suggests that post-stroke bimanual coordination impairment is closely related to selective damage to sensory feedback pathways, manifested as task-dependent reductions in ascending (muscle-to-cortex) corticomuscular coupling and compensatory cortical reorganization. Multimodal neurophysiological indicators may serve as potential quantitative tools for assessing upper limb function after stroke, but age-matched control studies are essential to dissociate stroke effects from aging effects.

item.title: Characteristics of visual search and prefrontal brain activity in individuals with autism spectrum disorder: functional near-infrared spectroscopy study.
item.description:
Brain & development
Introduction The term 'visual search' (VS) is used to describe behaviors such as finding a desired item while shopping or looking for a room key. These behaviors are important in everyday life. Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have been reported to experience difficulties with VS. However, the characteristics of VS and the associated brain activity remain unclear. Therefore, we investigated these characteristics in detail using a measurement method that combined VS tasks with brain function measurements. Methods Twenty-one individuals with ASD and 42 typically developing (TD) individuals, matched for age and visual intelligence, participated in this study. The characteristics of VS were evaluated using two types of cancellation tasks: structured and random arrays. We evaluated VS performance using various measurements, including the rate of intersections and the best r, which reflect systematicity and directional constancy. We measured brain activity using functional near-infrared spectroscopy in the prefrontal cortex (PFC). Results The ASD group had a significantly higher rate of intersections and a significantly lower best r than the TD group. The right PFC activity was significantly higher than the activity in other PFC regions during the random array task in the TD group. Additionally, the TD group exhibited significantly higher right PFC activity than the ASD group. Conclusion These results suggest that VS in individuals with ASD is characterized by inconsistent search direction and disorganization and that patterns of PFC brain activity during VS may also differ from those observed in TD individuals.

item.title: Multimodal evidence associated with 20Hz rTMS in AD: neuroaxonal injury reduction, neural oscillatory rebalancing, and multilayer network integration.
item.description:
Behavioural brain research
High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been demonstrated to enhance cognitive function in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the neurobiological mechanisms associated with neuroaxonal injury, neural oscillatory dynamics, and large-scale network reorganization remain unclear. In this study, we first conducted a randomized, sham-controlled trial with 16 patients with AD to evaluate the efficacy of DLPFC-targeted rTMS, followed by a single-arm multimodal cohort study of 30 patients to explore potential neurobiological mechanisms through cognitive assessments, blood biomarkers, EEG oscillatory activity, and multiplex brain network analysis. In Stage 1, the sham group showed no significant pre-post changes in MMSE or MoCA scores (MMSE: Z = -0.738, Cohen's r = 0.26; MoCA: Z =-0.853, Cohen's r = 0.30). The active rTMS group showed improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.124, Cohen's r = 0.75) and MoCA (Z = -2.108, Cohen's r = 0.75). In stage 2, rTMS was associated with improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.863, Cohen's r = 0.523) and MoCA (t = -6.137, Cohen's r = 0.752) scores. Biomarker analyses indicated a significant decrease in NfL concentrations (Z=-2.371, Cohen's r=0.484). EEG recordings revealed a decrease in delta power in the left temporal lobe (t=2.158, Cohen's r=0.372) and increases in beta power in the right parietal lobe and gamma power in the temporal lobe (beta: Z=-2.088, Cohen's r=0.381; gamma: Z=-2.129, Cohen's r=0.389). Network analysis showed reduced modularity and enhanced global efficiency across theta, alpha, and beta bands, accompanied by increased degree of overlap in frontal, parietal, and occipital regions. Importantly, MoCA improvement correlated with gamma-band global efficiency (R=0.389, P=0.034) and multilayer clustering coefficients in the left frontal and right occipital regions (R=0.478, P=0.008; R=0.398, P=0.029). Overall, rTMS exposure was associated with cognitive improvements in patients with AD, together with changes in neurodegeneration-related biomarkers and EEG network organization. These findings suggest that cognitive changes following rTMS may be associated with oscillatory modulation and large-scale network remodeling. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Registration number: ChiCTR2500095949; Registration Date: 2025-01-15.

item.title: Copy number variants across the developmental epilepsy-developmental and epileptic encephalopathy spectrum: an Indonesian case series.
item.description:
Neurogenetics
Developmental epilepsy (DE) and developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) comprise neurodevelopmental disorders in which epilepsy occurs alongside developmental impairment of varying contributions from the underlying etiology and epileptic activity. Advances in genetic testing, including whole-exome sequencing (WES), whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), have facilitated the identification of copy number variants (CNVs); however, data on CNV-associated epilepsy and neurodevelopmental disorders remain limited in Southeast Asia, including Indonesia. This retrospective case series describes the clinical and genetic characteristics of four Indonesian children across the DE-DEE spectrum with pathogenic CNVs identified at a tertiary referral hospital in Yogyakarta, Indonesia. Among 48 patients who underwent WES, CNVs were identified in five; four underwent further genetic characterization and were included in this case series, while one patient died before additional testing could be performed. Clinical manifestations included early-onset seizures, developmental delay or intellectual impairment, and abnormal EEG and/or neuroimaging findings. Genetic findings included a 2q24.3 deletion involving SCN1A in a patient with Dravet syndrome and 15q11.2-q13.1 deletions involving UBE3A in three patients with clinical features of Angelman syndrome. Confirmatory testing using WGS or CMA further characterized the identified CNVs. This case series expands the clinical and molecular data on pathogenic CNVs associated with pediatric epilepsy and neurodevelopmental disorders in an underrepresented Southeast Asian population and illustrates the complementary roles of sequencing and chromosomal analysis in genetic diagnosis.

item.title: The Concise Language Paradigm in left and right hemisphere stroke: a longitudinal source-localized EEG study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The mechanisms underlying language recovery after stroke remain poorly understood. Most previous studies have either focused on language comprehension or production and/or relied on hemodynamic measures, with limited complementary electrophysiological evidence. Here, we combined the Concise Language Paradigm (CLaP), assessing comprehension and production, with individualized electroencephalography (EEG) source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke language function and changes in hemispheric dominance over time. In two sessions, we tested stroke-free controls, individuals with left hemisphere (LH) or right hemisphere (RH) stroke. Participants with stroke were assessed two and seven months post-stroke. EEG data were analyzed using event-related potentials and time-frequency representations, followed by source reconstruction based on state-of-the-art individual MRI-derived forward models. Laterality indices were calculated to assess changes in hemispheric dominance between sessions. Behaviorally, the LH group showed low performance at two months followed by overall improvement, whereas the RH group mainly improved in functional communication. EEG activity was significantly modulated by task condition across comprehension and production contrasts. Source-level results in controls were consistent with established language-related networks, serving as regions of interest for the stroke analyses. In the stroke groups, hemispheric dominance differed between LH and RH stroke participants, with LH participants showing systematic shifts from left- to right-hemisphere dominance between sessions, if not already right-hemisphere dominant at two months. Our study provides evidence on comprehension and production performance after stroke using a single paradigm. These findings demonstrate dynamic changes in hemispheric dominance during post-stroke recovery, ultimately highlighting the value of individualized EEG source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke plasticity.

item.title: Characterization of Sleep, Spectral, and Epileptiform Activity in Individuals Aged 8-27 Years with SYNGAP1-Related Disorder Using an at-Home Dry EEG Headband
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
SYNGAP1-related disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is associated with sleep disturbances, seizures, and neurophysiological abnormalities. However, in-lab EEG can be difficult to obtain due to the behavioral and sensory disorders associated with this condition. In this study we collected EEG in SYNGAP1-RD participants (n=30 enrolled, 27 contributing data) in a decentralized protocol using a dry electrode headband as a path to longitudinal, research-grade data collection in this population. At-home data collection was successful with 180 recordings containing over 1 hour of usable data collected from 23 participants. Across these recordings, sporadic interictal epileptiform discharges were present in 22 of 23 participants but electrographic seizures were not observed. Relative to an adolescent control population (n=10), SYNGAP1-RD participants showed increased wake after sleep onset, reduced sleep efficiency, and decreased time in N1 and N3 sleep stages along with increased time in N2. We reproduced prior findings from awake spectral EEG analyses, including elevated broadband power along with reduced relative alpha power and alpha-theta ratio in the SYNGAP1 cohort. Notably, differences in spectral power were tightly linked to sleep stage, revealing sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics not previously characterized in SYNGAP1-RD. Finally, we examined differences between variants producing truncations downstream of the GAP domain and those producing truncations before or within it, but analyses were limited by a small sample size (n=4 for the post-GAP variant). Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of at-home multi-night sleep EEG collection in participants with SYNGAP1-RD and led to both corroborative and novel findings.

item.title: Single-Case Design for Network-based BCI Rehabilitation: Individual Learning Trajectories and Effects of Motor Imagery Timing in Stroke Patients
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are increasingly investigated for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, it remains unclear how BCI control improves through repeated training in stroke patients and whether the timing of MI decoding systematically influences this trajectory. To address this question, we implemented a single-case experimental design involving five chronic stroke patients enrolling in a longitudinal electroencephalography MI-BCI training involving their affected hand. Across 18 sessions conducted over six weeks, the onset of a fixed-duration MI decoding window was randomized to occur 1, 2, or 3~s after cue onset according to an alternating-treatments single-case design. Notably, the BCI combined spectral power and functional connectivity features to classify MI states. The MI classification timing had no significant effect on BCI accuracy, fatigue, or spasticity. BCI accuracy increased across training in four of five patients and was accompanied by patient-specific longitudinal changes in local spectral activity and functional connectivity. These convergent trajectories were consistent with acquisition of BCI control, but were not accompanied by clinically meaningful improvement in motor function. Varying the onset of the MI decoding window provided no systematic benefit for BCI control. Instead, differences in neurophysiological trajectories across patients indicate that MI decoding parameters need to be personalized and reassessed throughout the training. Overall, these findings inform more individualized and effective BCI settings for neuromotor stroke rehabilitation.

item.title: APOE ε4 carriage is associated with pallido-putaminal diffusion alterations in early Parkinson’s disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract APOE ε4 may influence Parkinson’s disease (PD) progression, but its microstructural correlates remain unclear. We examined 75 early drug-naïve PD patients (25 ε4 carriers) and 46 healthy controls (HC; 16 ε4 carriers) from the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative using ROI and voxel-wise diffusion tensor imaging analyses. Within PD, ε4 carriers showed higher pallidal mean, radial and axial diffusivity and lower pallidal and putaminal fractional anisotropy. Voxel-wise analyses localized differences to left pallido-putaminal clusters. HC showed no significant APOE -related differences. In exploratory analyses across the overall PD sample, higher cluster radial diffusivity was associated with higher serum neurofilament light chain at baseline (β = 0.395, p = 0.001) and across two years, without evidence of moderation by APOE genotype or association with longitudinal change. These findings link APOE ε4 to regional diffusion differences in early PD without detectable subcortical volume differences. Their disease specificity and prognostic relevance remain to be established.

item.title: Reassessment of the DTI-ALPS index in focal epilepsy.
item.description:
European radiology experimental
Objective Recent evidence highlights the limited specificity of diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) along perivascular spaces (ALPS) as a noninvasive glymphatic biomarker because microstructural tract degeneration and crossing-fiber geometry confound it. We aimed to reassess the interpretation of the DTI-ALPS index in people with focal epilepsy. Materials and methods Seventy-nine people with drug-resistant focal epilepsy (PWFE) underwent comprehensive presurgical work-up and 3-T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Etiologies included MRI-negative epilepsy, malformations of cortical development, temporal lobe epilepsy, and low-grade epilepsy-associated tumors. DTI preprocessing was conducted using QSIPrep with automated region-of-interest (ROI) placement. Linear regression models and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to assess group differences and associations with clinical variables. Twenty-five age- and sex-matched healthy controls were included for comparison. Results Seventy-nine patients (28.6 years ± 11.3 [mean ± standard deviation]; 47 men, 32 women) and 25 healthy controls (mean age, 26.7 years ± 4.2; 11 men, 14 women) were evaluated. DTI-ALPS findings were more abnormal in lesions in proximity to the ROI (p = 0.014), implicating local white matter disruption as a modifier, which was further corroborated by reduced postoperative values. No associations were identified with disease duration, sex, or normalized gray-or white matter volumes. Conclusion Our results demonstrate a distance-dependent correlation of DTI-ALPS values to the seizure onset zone in focal epilepsy, whilst no significant associations to disease duration or normalized brain volumes were found. Together, these findings suggest that local disruption of fiber tracts may act as important modifiers of this measure and warrant caution in the interpretation of the DTI-ALPS index. Key points Question Microstructural changes may significantly confound the interpretation of the DTI-ALPS index as a surrogate parameter for glymphatic system dysfunction in epilepsy. Findings No significant differences in the DTI-ALPS index were observed comparing PWFE with healthy controls; however, lesion proximity and post-operative status significantly alter the metric. Relevance statement Local white-matter disruption and microstructural architecture may significantly alter the DTI-ALPS index; therefore, caution is warranted when interpreting the index as a glymphatic biomarker in focal epilepsy.

item.title: Channel-Adaptive Temporal Modeling with Grouped Convolutional Network and Informer for Seizure Detection and Prediction.
item.description:
International journal of neural systems
Reliable identification and early prediction of epileptic seizures play a critical role in improving patient outcomes and supporting timely therapeutic decision-making. To address the challenges of spatiotemporal feature coupling and long-range dependency modeling in multi-channel EEG signals, this paper proposes a channel-adaptive temporal modeling framework named GCNN-Informer. The framework follows a three-stage pipeline: a grouped convolutional network (GCNN) extracts local features and selects the five most discriminative channels; a convolutional block attention module (CBAM) performs dual spatiotemporal enhancement; and a lightweight Informer encoder captures global temporal dependencies via the ProbSparse self-attention mechanism. Experiments on the CHB-MIT dataset, conducted under a patient-specific evaluation scheme, demonstrated that the proposed method achieved accuracies of 97.33% for seizure detection and 97.28% for seizure prediction, with a low false detection rate (FDR) of 0.30/h and a false prediction rate (FPR) of 0.03/h. Grad-CAM visualization further shows that as EEG signals evolve from normal/interictal to preictal and then to ictal stages, the model's attention heatmap progressively transitions from locally sparse highlighting to continuous block-like highlighting, and finally to dense deep-red responses - a pattern that closely aligns with clinical electrophysiological dynamics. This study provides an accurate and generalizable deep-learning solution for real-time epileptic monitoring and early-warning systems.

item.title: Multimodal associations between posterior hippocampus glutamate metabolism, visual cortex connectivity, and intrusive trauma reexperiencing symptoms.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Hippocampal dysfunction is implicated in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), particularly intrusive reexperiencing symptoms, and may be mediated by glutamatergic excitotoxicity. Markers of glutamate dysfunction (higher glutamate to N-acetyl aspartate levels; Glu/NAA) in the hippocampus (HPC) have been linked to reexperiencing symptoms. However, the HPC demonstrates heterogeneity along its anterior-posterior axis, with different functional connectivity patterns and PTSD symptom associations, motivating investigations into glutamate metabolism in anterior and posterior HPC subregions (a/pHPC). To this end, 121 symptomatic trauma-exposed adults with current trauma reexperiencing symptoms completed magnetic resonance spectroscopy and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging to examine the regional specificity of HPC Glu/NAA associations with reexperiencing symptoms and the link to a/pHPC functional connectivity. PTSD symptoms were assessed with the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5. Reexperiencing symptom severity was associated with greater Glu/NAA in the pHPC, but not aHPC. pHPC Glu/NAA was further linked to stronger functional connectivity between the pHPC and visual cortex (VC), which in turn correlated with more severe reexperiencing symptoms. This strengthened pHPC-VC connectivity explained the shared variance between pHPC Glu/NAA and reexperiencing severity, suggesting dysregulated glutamate metabolism in the pHPC may contribute to reexperiencing symptoms through functional connectivity with the VC. These findings replicate prior work linking HPC Glu/NAA to trauma reexperiencing symptoms and provide novel evidence of this association in the pHPC, but not aHPC, which is mediated by its functional connectivity with the VC. This multimodal investigation supports translational models of glutamatergic dysfunction in trauma-related disorders and highlights new targets for pharmacological and neuromodulatory interventions.

item.title: Impact of cannabis use and cannabis composition on formal thought disorder and related brain networks: An fMRI study in 51 patients with schizophrenia.
item.description:
Schizophrenia research
Background Formal thought disorder (FTD) is a core dimension of schizophrenia, which has been associated in previous studies with increased brain functional connectivity between temporal gyri and striatal regions as measured with fMRI. Cannabis use is highly prevalent in schizophrenia population as compared with the general population and, in the context of elevated tetrahydrocannabinol/cannabidiol (THC/CBD) ratio, has been found to be associated with increased FTD in schizophrenia. Consequently, in this study, we aimed to investigate whether cannabis consumption in patients with schizophrenia is generally associated with both enhanced functional connectivity and FTD. Methods We explored the functional connectivity between the temporal gyri and striatal regions in 51 schizophrenia patients divided into two groups stratified by cannabis use. FTD was measured using the conceptual disorganization item from the Positive And Negative Syndrome Scale. Region-of-interest (ROI)-to-ROI and seed-based connectivity analyses, correlation tests, and mediation models were conducted using both frequentist and Bayesian approaches. Results No significant difference was found in terms of functional connectivity between cannabis users and non-users. THC/CBD ratio was not significantly associated with cortico-striatal connectivity or FTD. Overall, Bayesian results indicated moderate to strong evidence favoring the null hypothesis across most models. Conclusion Cannabis use was not robustly associated with an altered cortico-striatal connectivity in this sample. The convergence of frequentist and Bayesian evidence suggests that cannabis use may not account for previously reported FTD-related connectivity alterations in schizophrenia. Larger studies considering cannabis composition, dose-response relationships, and symptom dimensions are warranted to refine these findings.

item.title: Implementation and early experience with tubular retractor-assisted minimally invasive parafascicular surgery for deep brain tumors.
item.description:
Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
Minimally invasive parafascicular surgery using tubular retractors (tr-MIPS) has emerged as a strategy to access deep intra-axial lesions while minimizing white matter disruption. However, practical guidance on institutional implementation and integration with modern intraoperative adjuncts remains limited. We describe our early institutional experience with tr-MIPS, with a focus on workflow adoption, multimodal adjunct integration, and feasibility. Demographic, radiographic, operative, and postoperative data were collected, with particular attention to extent of resection, neurological outcomes, and use of adjunctive technologies. Six patients underwent tr-MIPS for deep intra-axial tumors of varied histology. Gross or near-total resection was achieved in four cases. Five patients experienced no new postoperative neurological deficits, and one had transient dysphasia. Median length of stay was 3.5 days. A range of adjuncts including diffusion tensor imaging, 5-aminolevulinic acid fluorescence, intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring, and depth-electrode electroencephalography were successfully incorporated without workflow disruption. Notably, intraoperative depth-electrode EEG was used to guide resection of an epileptogenic lesion, representing a novel adjunctive application in the tr-MIPS setting. tr-MIPS can be implemented within a modern neurosurgical practice and feasibly integrated with multiple intraoperative adjuncts. We demonstrate feasibility with the addition of this technique to our center's armamentarium. Beyond facilitating access to deep lesions, its compatibility with technologies such as tractography, neurophysiologic monitoring, and EEG expands its functional utility. These findings support the feasibility of a broader adoption of tr-MIPS and highlight opportunities for multimodal, precision-guided minimally invasive neuro-oncologic surgery.

item.title: Electrocorticographic Network Feature Space Constriction as a Preictal Biomarker.
item.description:
Neuroinformatics
In patients with epilepsy, seizures are associated with pathological neural synchronization. However, the preictal period preceding a seizure often exhibits reduced spatial synchronization compared to normal cognition. This observation aligns with the concept of the brain as a complex dynamical system, where a reduction in dimensionality and resilience can precede a phase transition. The Critical Brain Hypothesis suggests a connection between the loss of healthy scale-free behavior and various disorders, including epilepsy. Our study investigates preictal changes by utilizing network features, such as mean node degree and mean clustering coefficient, derived from thresholded correlation matrices of patient intracranial electrocorticographic electrode data. We observed a suppression of intermittent high-synchronization periods within the feature space during the minutes leading up to seizure onset. This constriction of the explored hypervolume in the preictal state indicates a breakdown in the brain's ability to maintain normal coherence. We use these preictal changes to predict the probability of seizure onset using a Support Vector Machine algorithm. These discrete predictions can then be combined into real-time continuous seizure risk forecasts via Bayesian updating. This innovative and computationally lightweight approach has the potential to significantly improve upon static predictions, providing opportunities for more adaptable, quantitative, and interpretable tools for managing seizures.

item.title: Stability of the Epileptogenic Index across seizures and the effects of sleep and withdrawal of anti-seizure medications.
item.description:
Epilepsia open
Objective Epileptogenic Index (EI) is a promising index to evaluate the epileptogenicity of the brain tissue and is useful in planning epilepsy surgery. We aimed to evaluate whether EI maps are consistent across seizures within patients and whether EI-derived measures are affected by the vigilance state and anti-seizure medication (ASM) dose. Methods We analyzed 127 stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) seizures from 19 patients. EI was calculated in all seizures. Within-patient EI consistency was assessed using pairwise Spearman correlations between seizure-specific EI maps. To assess the effects of vigilance and ASM on EI consistency, we calculated a contact-level p_weighted EI score that combines the frequency of suprathreshold EI involvement and mean EI magnitude, separately across vigilance states and in a subset of patients with different ASM states. Results Mean seizure-to-seizure EI correlations ranged from 0.11 to 0.81, indicating substantial variability in within-patient EI consistency. Seven patients showed high consistency (≥0.6) and four showed low consistency (≤0.3). At the contact level, no differences in p_weighted EI were found between wakefulness and sleep. In contrast, p_weighted EI was significantly higher during reduced ASM compared with full ASM doses. Significance EI maps are not uniformly stable across seizures. ASM reduction may broaden or intensify EI-defined epileptogenic involvement, suggesting that ASM status should be considered when interpreting EI during SEEG evaluation. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation to determine their clinical utility for surgical planning. Plain language summary The Epileptogenic Index (EI) measures the involvement of a recorded brain area during a specific seizure. This study shows that EI patterns can vary significantly between different seizures in the same patient. While sleep states do not change these patterns, reducing a patient's anti-seizure medications increases EI values, making seizures appear to spread more broadly. These medication-induced changes must be carefully considered to accurately map the epileptic network for surgical decisions.

item.title: Movement-specific effects of transcranial magnetic stimulation over premotor and parietal cortices after stroke
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has been proposed to support post-stroke motor recovery, but the response may depend on the task and motor-network status. We aimed to compare how premotor and parietal stimulation affects performance across reach directions with different movement demands, in preparation for therapeutic application of TMS. Methods: 16 participants with chronic subcortical stroke performed planar reaches with the KINARM exoskeleton toward distal and proximal targets. Before movement, a 10-Hz triple-pulse TMS train was delivered over bilateral dorsal or ventral premotor cortex (PMd, PMv) or dorsomedial posterior parietal cortex (PPC) at subthreshold and suprathreshold intensities. The parietal midline was used as the control target. Participant-level bootstrap confidence intervals assessed changes in trajectory straightness and smoothness relative to the control target and differences between reach directions. We compared motor-network activity and connectivity using task-based and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from participants with stroke and neurologically intact controls. To explore response variability, we tested associations between TMS response and motor impairment, resting-state connectivity, and the change in task-evoked activity at the stimulated region from planning to movement. Results: Suprathreshold PMd and PPC stimulation in both hemispheres improved trajectory straightness or smoothness during distal reaches relative to the control target. Suprathreshold contralesional PMd stimulation increased trajectory deviation and reduced smoothness during proximal reaches. Baseline performance during distal reaches was more closely related to motor impairment, and contralesional PMd effects were more favorable during distal than proximal reaches across all kinematic measures. Participants with stroke showed lower bilateral PMv activation during movement and stronger interhemispheric PPC connectivity. Only the change in task-evoked activity at the stimulated region from planning to movement was related to TMS response. Smaller changes relative to controls were associated with more favorable kinematic effects during distal reaches. Conclusions: Movements more affected after stroke were the most responsive to this type of stimulation. The response to TMS was also associated with task-evoked activity differences at the stimulated region between movement planning and execution. Neuromodulation may therefore be most effective when designed around both the pathophysiology of the cortical target and the type of movement.

item.title: Cortical physiological arousal following termination of absence seizures
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Although the brain state preceding and during absence seizures has been well-characterized, the postictal brain state remains largely unexplored due to the prevailing assumption that absence seizures have minimal or no postictal changes. To address this gap, scalp EEG recordings from 55 patients with 3-4 Hz spike-wave discharges across four multi-site cohorts were analyzed. Spectral power was measured relative to each seizure's preictal baseline, and the postictal period was compared to a time-matched preictal window. Rather than an immediate return to baseline after seizure offset, a significant broadband increase in EEG power was observed in the gamma (>25 Hz) and delta (<4 Hz) frequency bands, followed by a gradual decline over the next 15 s to 30 s. In contrast, no comparable change preceded the seizures. This suggests that recovery from an absence seizure is an active process with a characteristic electrophysiological signature consistent with cortical activation and arousal. Thus, postictal arousal may facilitate exit from the seizure state, and with further work could serve as an electrophysiological marker and therapeutic target for recovery in absence epilepsy.

item.title: Localising the Seizure Onset Zone from Routine Interictal and Ictal Scalp EEG Via a Factorised Spatiotemporal Ensemble Deep Learning Framework
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Drug-resistant focal epilepsy requires precise localisation of the epileptogenic zone (EZ) for surgical resection. Current practice depends on invasive recordings or spontaneous seizure capture, a costly and risky bottleneck. Interictal scalp EEG can exhibit localising features like spikes, but scalp EEG suffers from volume conduction (the smearing of brain signals across multiple electrodes) and low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which obscure subtle spatial dynamics. Neurophysiologist review of long, often multi-day recordings is time-consuming and expertise-dependent, and while computational methods exist, they tend to rely heavily on human-designed features. Deep learning for EEG localisation could therefore help to improve clinical efficiency and sensitivity. Objectives: To develop and validate a non-invasive deep learning approach for lobar-level localisation of the seizure onset zone (SOZ), the primary electrophysiological proxy for the epileptogenic zone (EZ), using interictal and ictal segments from routine scalp EEG. The model is trained on expert-annotated clinical labels and is intended to augment, not supplant, clinical judgement in EZ delineation. Methods: We curated 262 sessions (6,000+ hours) from 100 patients with unilateral focal epilepsy, tested with an extra 28-patient internal and a 9-patient external dataset. The framework integrates: (1) an online augmentation pipeline (Gaussian noise, amplitude scaling, temporal cropping, and hemispheric channel swap) to mitigate overfitting. (2) a multi-scale temporal block for 20-200 ms discharge morphologies; (3) a factorised spatiotemporal Transformer decoupling temporal and spatial attention to counter volume conduction; and (4) a hemispheric mutual exclusivity penalty encoding unilateral priors. A five-model heterogeneous ensemble, fused via model soup, was evaluated on held-out, seizure-free, and cross-institutional cohorts. Results: The ensemble achieved 88.46% session-level exact match on internal test data, outperforming EEGNet (50.00%). Performance generalised to the seizure-free holdout set (82.76%) and to cross-institutional data (84.62%). Rare occipital class (RO) recall rose from 0.500 to 1.000, with zero false positives on healthy controls (n=108). On unlabelled random segments, accuracy was 66.67% (vs. 14% chance). A full 24-hour recording was processed in 4.26 minutes, with inference under 8 seconds, highlighting localising windows for targeted expert clinical review Conclusion: Clinically actionable SOZ spatial information is encoded in routine interictal scalp EEG. Our factorised ensemble provides a safe, interpretable, and efficient tool to expedite presurgical evaluation, potentially reducing reliance on prolonged monitoring and invasive implantation.

item.title: Acute scalp EEG signatures of anterior thalamic DBS in epilepsy:reproducible gamma power enhancement within an aperiodic spectral-state shift
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) is an established treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy, but acute scalp-EEG signatures of stimulation remain incompletely characterized. Objective: To identify acute scalp-EEG signatures of ANT-DBS and assess their cross-year reproducibility in a proof-of-concept repeated-session cohort. Methods: Scalp EEG from five patients recorded one year apart (10 sessions) was analyzed during nominal cyclic DBS (1 s ON, ~5 s OFF). DBS ON was compared with the within-cycle OFFmean and consecutive post-offset OFF windows using power spectral density (PSD), spatiotemporal-frequency (STF) analysis, and spectral parameterization. Results: DBS ON showed higher 30-70 Hz gamma power than OFFmean in all sessions (median +0.94 dB), with significant PSD clusters overlapping gamma in 10/10 sessions. STF identified gamma increases as the most reproducible spatiotemporal effect. Exploratory frontal 34-44 Hz and central 56-70 Hz components showed cross-year support, and the broader pattern persisted when 48-52 or 45-55 Hz were excluded before clustering. Lower-frequency effects were more heterogeneous and weakened from early to late OFF windows. Aperiodic parameterization showed lower ON exponent and offset in all sessions (Delta chi = -0.20; Delta b = -0.25). After correction, theta suppression was not preserved, whereas a smaller low-gamma residual remained. Conclusions: ANT-DBS was associated with consistent acute scalp-EEG state signatures comprising raw gamma enhancement, lower aperiodic exponent and offset, and a modest residual low-gamma effect. These hypothesis-generating findings show that scalp EEG can capture acute ANT-DBS state changes, while larger prospective studies are needed to establish clinical relevance.

item.title: Preoperative diffusion-perivascular MRI burden and postoperative delirium after subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation in Parkinson disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Postoperative delirium after subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation may reflect pre-existing brain vulnerability, but the preoperative imaging correlates of this vulnerability remain uncertain. We examined whether a combined diffusion and perivascular imaging burden was associated with delirium after bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation. This single-centre observational cohort included 100 patients with Parkinson disease undergoing bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation and 32 healthy controls scanned with the same preoperative MRI protocol. Delirium was assessed during postoperative days using the Nursing Delirium Screening Scale with clinical adjudication. Age- and sex-adjusted reference models fitted in healthy controls were used to standardise tract diffusion metrics, diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space, and basal ganglia enlarged perivascular space counts. Directionally aligned diffusion and perivascular scores were averaged with equal domain weights. Patients who developed postoperative delirium (n = 30) had higher combined burden than those who did not (n = 70; 95% CI, 0.584 to 1.526; q<.001). Using Firth penalised logistic regression, higher combined burden remained associated with postoperative delirium after adjustment for age, sex, education, Mini-Mental State Examination score, disease duration, and motor severity (95% CI, 1.49 to 4.25; Wald P<.001). Higher burden was also associated with longer delirium duration and higher peak screening scores among affected patients. Exploratory internal prediction yielded an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.701 after adding burden to clinical variables, compared with 0.538 for clinical variables alone. These findings support preoperative diffusion-perivascular burden as a candidate marker of perioperative neuropsychiatric vulnerability requiring multicentre validation.

item.title: A Dual-Stream Spatio-Temporal Network with Bidirectional Rectification for Differential Diagnosis of Dementia using EEG
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Accurate differential diagnosis between Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is of critical importance for the early screening of neurodegenerative diseases. Scalp electroencephalogram (EEG), as a non-invasive neurophysiological detection tool with excellent temporal resolution, has been widely adopted in dementia screening research. However, the inherent low signal-to-noise ratio and non-stationarity of scalp EEG signals, combined with the highly overlapping pathological rhythms between AD and FTD patients, render existing single-domain representation methods incapable of achieving precise pathological differentiation. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a dual-stream spatio-temporal network. In this framework, multiscale temporal features and effective connectivity graph features are extracted in parallel, followed by their integration. However, directly fusing the features from the two streams tends to amplify their respective noises. Therefore, the Spatio-Temporal Feature Fusion Based on Bidirectional Rectification module is proposed to execute dynamic noise suppression on the features and subsequently performs deep feature fusion via a cross-attention mechanism. Furthermore, this paper applies knowledge distillation using attention maps to address the issue of imbalanced sample distributions in the dataset. Experimental results on the ADFTD-RS dataset show that the proposed framework yields a subject-level accuracy of 60.00\% and an F1-score of 57.44\%, showing measurable improvements over several baseline methods. This work offers a feasible approach for the computer-aided differential diagnosis of dementia based on resting-state EEG.

item.title: Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above ~60 Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. Furthermore, we derived an analytical formula for idealized neuron models which can approximately predict the tES sensitivity of different cell types at any given frequency. By characterizing the role of morphology and stimulation frequency in determining tES responses of single cells, this is an important step towards a better understanding of tES at the fundamental level. These results also provide an efficient and accurate method for characterizing and comparing the tES responses of different neural populations across the frequency spectrum, which facilitates optimizing tES for cell-type specific targeting.

item.title: DTI-Associated Blood Biomarkers in a Human Perioperative Brain Perturbation Model.
item.description:
Journal of neurotrauma
Circulating biomarkers of brain perturbation are rarely evaluated against anatomically localized in vivo imaging measures, limiting biological interpretation. We tested whether perioperative changes in candidate biomarkers were associated with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)-defined microstructural changes in a controlled human perioperative model. In a paired cohort of 75 patients undergoing left-sided encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis, we obtained matched pre- and postoperative DTI and blood samples. Six biomarkers (ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase-L1 [UCH-L1], glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP], S100 calcium-binding protein B [S100B], neurofilament light chain, neuron-specific enolase, and protein tau) were quantified. Analyses included paired comparisons, region-of-interest-based cross-modal correlations, sparse canonical correlation analysis (sCCA) with bootstrap stability assessment, and patient-grouped regularized logistic regression for state discrimination. DTI showed perioperative changes in bilateral temporal-limbic regions and connected white matter, with the largest effects in left hippocampal and amygdalar territories on the operated side. UCH-L1, GFAP, and S100B showed the clearest paired increases and dominated internal perioperative-state discrimination. Blood-DTI associations were heterogeneous across biomarkers and states, and paired-change associations were not confined to these three markers. An observed three-biomarker panel discriminated perioperative state with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.914 in the test set. Several circulating biomarkers covaried with regional DTI measures in this exploratory perioperative cohort. UCH-L1, GFAP, and S100B were the most perioperatively responsive and state-discriminative markers, but the DTI-association pattern was not specific to this trio. The findings support a structure-associated framework for evaluating blood biomarkers against regional imaging changes; they do not validate these biomarkers for traumatic brain injury, and relevance to traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains hypothesis-generating.

item.title: Multimodal Analysis of Brain Network Abnormalities in Autism Spectrum Disorder: a Graph Neural Network-based Fusion Investigation of EEG and fNIRS.
item.description:
IEEE transactions on bio-medical engineering
Objective This study aimed to identify brain network abnormalities of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) by analyzing multimodal neuroimaging data through graph neural networks (GNNs), laying a technical foundation for future machine learning-based neuroimaging analysis. Methods We employed combined electroencephalogram (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to capture brain activity of 58 ASD children and 63 age- and gender-matched typically developing (TD) children. The concurrent EEG and fNIRS data were fused using an enhanced GNN to identify ASD with high accuracy. Key connections and regions of interest (ROIs) were identified for each group, followed by graph theory metrics (e.g., local efficiency) and topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify group differences. Results The proposed GNN model achieved 84% accuracy, outperforming the single-modality approach. Analysis of subgraph created by the model showed that the two groups exhibited different neural patterns in motor-language integration and lateralization, a key basis for GNN models to distinguish between the two groups. Individuals with ASD may also have topological defects such as lower average local efficiency and a lack of high-order structures. Conclusion The proposed framework effectively captures quantitative insights ranging from specific connection-level variations to network-level differences, identifying candidate discriminative connectivity patterns within this cohort. Significance This study establishes a multimodal deep learning framework that identifies candidate discriminative topological signatures from fused EEG-fNIRS data, providing preliminary within-cohort classification evidence and an exploratory topological analysis framework.

item.title: Neural sensitivity to peer rejection predicts depressive symptoms and daily mood in adolescents.
item.description:
NPP - digital psychiatry and neuroscience
Understanding the role of peer feedback, particularly rejection, is critical for adolescent major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the neurophysiological markers core to peer feedback, especially those that may presage risk for depression, are unclear. Adolescents (N = 179; ages 13-18; healthy controls n = 62, remitted MDD n = 80, current MDD n = 37) completed a baseline clinical assessment and a revised Chatroom Task during EEG recording, from which the P3 to peer acceptance and rejection feedback was quantified. Over 12 months, daily mood and keyboard inputs from adolescents' smartphones were passively obtained. Linear models evaluated whether the P3 difference between rejection and acceptance (ΔP3) prospectively predicted depressive severity and average daily mood. Exploratory natural language processing examined whether friendship-focused social communication moderated the association between neural sensitivity to peer feedback and subsequent clinical outcomes. Group and feedback type interacted in predicting P3 amplitude (F(2176) = 4.84, p = 0.009): adolescents with current MDD showed larger P3 amplitudes to rejection than acceptance, whereas remitted MDD showed elevated amplitudes to both feedback types relative to controls. In a general linear model adjusting for age, sex, site, and baseline depression severity, the Group × ΔP3 interaction was significant in predicting severity at follow-up (b = 0.092, p = 0.045); higher ΔP3 predicted higher follow-up severity in current MDD, but not in remitted MDD or healthy controls. Across the full sample, larger ΔP3 was associated with lower average daily mood over 12 months (b = -1.673, p = 0.045). These findings suggest that enhanced neural sensitivity to peer rejection may be deeply engrained in adolescent depression, shaping both the longitudinal course of depressive symptoms and daily mood.

item.title: Gamma-band network segregation links corollary discharge dysfunction and anomalous self-experiences in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Schizophrenia research
Anomalous self-experiences (ASEs) are a core feature of psychotic disorders and reflect disturbances in ipseity. Impairments in corollary discharge mechanism have been proposed as a neurobiological substrate of ASEs, and an imbalance between brain network integration and segregation, may impair the coherent flow of mental contents, thereby disrupting their fluid and implicit character. However, the relationship between corollary discharge and functional network properties has not been directly examined. This link was assessed in thirty participants with schizophrenia and thirty healthy controls. Functional network was computed using the Phase Locking Value (PLV) from resting-state EEG in the gamma band and two parameters were calculated: the clustering coefficient (ClC, as a proxy for segregation) and the path length (PL, as a proxy for integration); corollary discharge was indexed by N1 suppression in a talk-listen paradigm; and ASEs were evaluated using the 'Inventory of Psychotic-Like Anomalous Self-Experiences' (IPASE) total score. Patients with schizophrenia showed significantly greater gamma-band network segregation and lower integration than healthy controls. Moreover, higher segregation in this band was associated with reduced N1 suppression and greater ASEs severity in patients, whereas network integration was not associated with N1 suppression nor ASEs. These findings suggest that excessive gamma-band network segregation may be correlated with disrupted corollary discharge functioning and may compromise the distinction between self-generated and external stimuli. Therefore, it may alter the sense of ipseity by interfering with the integration of mental contents into the flow of consciousness, thereby contributing to greater severity of ASEs.

item.title: Altered white matter functional activity and connectivity in pretreatment breast cancer: exploratory associations with affective symptoms.
item.description:
Brain research bulletin
Objective Resting-state fMRI studies in breast cancer have predominantly focused on gray matter, with limited attention to white matter functional organization. This study investigated white matter functional activity and connectivity before treatment and their associations with anxiety and depressive symptoms. Methods Female patients with breast cancer (BC) were recruited from Zhejiang Provincial Tongde Hospital from November 2023 to December 2025. Amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF) and fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (fALFF) were used to compare local white matter functional activity between the BC and healthy control (HC) groups. Seed-based functional connectivity (FC) analysis was then performed to investigate whole-brain white matter FC alterations. Correlations between clinical scale scores and rs-fMRI indices were analyzed. Results Compared with HCs, patients with BC showed altered ALFF/fALFF in the anterior and posterior corona radiata, internal capsule, posterior thalamic radiation, body of the corpus callosum, pontine crossing tract, left superior cerebellar peduncle, and left superior longitudinal fasciculus. Seed-based analysis revealed decreased FC within the bilateral anterior corona radiata and between the body of the corpus callosum and right anterior corona radiata, and increased FC between the left superior cerebellar peduncle and left posterior thalamic radiation. Higher ALFF in the body of the corpus callosum and reduced FC between this region and the right anterior corona radiata were associated with higher Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores at an uncorrected threshold. Neither association survived FDR correction. Conclusion Patients with BC showed altered white matter functional activity and connectivity before cancer-related treatment, suggesting that pretreatment brain functional alterations may also involve white matter functional organization. The relationship between these white matter changes and anxiety or depressive symptoms remains exploratory.

item.title: Attention Load Modulates Functional Brain Connectivity Reorganization in Children with High Autistic Traits: Evidence from Phase and Amplitude Coupling Metrics.
item.description:
Behavioural brain research
Whether emotional processing difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) stem from deficits in recognizing emotional stimuli or from limitations in flexibly reorganizing brain networks under increasing cognitive demands remains an open question. To our knowledge, this study is among the first to investigate the effects of graded attentional load (low/moderate/high) on EEG-based functional connectivity and brain network organization during task-irrelevant emotional prosody processing in children with high autistic traits (n = 31), by integrating phase-based (iPLV, wPLI) and amplitude-based (AEC) metrics together with graph-theoretic indices within a unified analytic framework. Connectivity matrices from a sliding-window approach were decomposed into edge-level, distributional, and graph-theoretic features and load-dependent changes in connectivity were assessed with statistical analyzes and classification models. The results suggested that attentional load did not uniformly increase or decrease connectivity but rather produced a multi-layered pattern of reorganization that varied as a function of frequency band, connectivity metric, and network topology. Phase-based connectivity in the beta band was decreased with increasing load, while amplitude envelope coupling (AEC) in the theta and alpha bands was increased under high load. This dual-mechanism pattern was most pronounced under the high-load condition, which yielded the greatest number of nominally significant features (uncorrected p<0.05; none survived FDR correction), the largest theta-AEC effect size (Kendall's W up to 0.22), and the best-performing classification model among those tested (accuracy = 72.6%, F1 = 0.725, AUC = 0.764). In conclusion, this exploratory study suggests that, in children with high autistic traits, increasing cognitive demands may be associated with band-specific network reorganization characterized by attenuated phase-based coordination alongside enhanced amplitude-based coupling; these patterns did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, have not been compared with those of typically developed children, and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. If replicated, such findings could eventually inform how environmental stimulation and cognitive load are structured in special education settings.

item.title: Dissociable associations of free-water fraction and DTI-ALPS index with disease manifestation and mutation carrier status in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Japanese journal of radiology
Purpose Parkinson's disease (PD) is a biologically heterogeneous disorder. Diffusion MRI-derived free-water fraction (FWf ) and DTI-ALPS index have been proposed as biomarkers of PD-related brain alterations; however, their relationships with clinical disease manifestation and genetic susceptibility remain unclear. This study investigated whether substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) FWf and DTI-ALPS indices show different associations with disease status and mutation carrier status across the PD continuum. Materials and methods Diffusion MRI data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative were analyzed, including healthy controls (HCs), non-manifesting mutation carriers (NMCs), and patients with sporadic or genetic PD. A 2 × 2 factorial analysis of covariance was performed to assess the effects of disease status and mutation carrier status on SNc FWf and DTI-ALPS indices. Exploratory longitudinal associations between baseline imaging measures and 4-year clinical outcomes were examined using multivariable linear regression with adjustment for the corresponding baseline clinical measures. Results Among 284 participants (63 HCs, 48 NMCs, 126 sporadic PD patients, and 47 genetic PD patients), mean SNc FWf showed a significant main effect of disease status, whereas mutation carrier status and the interaction effect were not significant. Sporadic PD patients exhibited higher SNc FWf than HCs and NMCs. In contrast, the left-sided DTI-ALPS index was associated with mutation carrier status. NMCs had lower left-sided DTI-ALPS indices than HCs and sporadic PD patients. In the exploratory longitudinal analysis, higher baseline mean SNc FWf was associated with a higher 4-year MDS-UPDRS Part II score, although this association was not significant when the analysis was restricted to participants with manifest PD. Conclusions SNc FWf and DTI-ALPS may capture complementary aspects of PD heterogeneity. SNc FWf appears more closely related to clinical disease expression, whereas DTI-ALPS index may reflect differences associated with genetic susceptibility. Further validation in larger mutation-stratified and longitudinal cohorts is warranted.

item.title: Glymphatic dysfunction in early-onset schizophrenia: DTI-ALPS index reduction tracks illness burden and is independently associated with cognitive performance in treatment-resistant patients.
item.description:
European child & adolescent psychiatry
Early-onset schizophrenia (EOS) is associated with greater cognitive impairment than adult-onset disease, and many patients also develop treatment resistance. Glymphatic dysfunction has been described in adult schizophrenia but not in EOS or in relation to treatment resistance. We used diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) to assess glymphatic function in 30 adolescents with EOS (15 treatment-resistant, TRS; 15 non-treatment-resistant, nTRS) and 29 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC). Participants completed a neuropsychological battery covering verbal memory, processing speed, executive function, working memory, verbal fluency, and social cognition. ALPS differed across groups (F(2,56) = 34.66, p < 0.001, η² = 0.553), with values decreasing from HC (1.625 ± 0.072) to nTRS (1.501 ± 0.098) to TRS (1.439 ± 0.048); the TRS-nTRS difference was not significant (d = 0.81, p = 0.066). Patients showed broad cognitive deficits relative to HC, but nTRS and TRS did not differ on any measure after FDR correction. ALPS showed a nominal inverse association with the number of psychotic episodes (ρ = -0.391, p = 0.033) but was unrelated to PANSS scores or antipsychotic dose. Within TRS, ALPS was independently associated with phonemic verbal fluency (COWAT: β = +0.74, p = 0.003); a parallel association with categorical fluency (β = +0.88, p < 0.001) was partly driven by an influential observation and is exploratory. Glymphatic dysfunction appears to be a disease-intrinsic feature of EOS, lowest in TRS, possibly linked to cumulative episodes rather than current symptoms, and may contribute to cognitive impairment in treatment-resistant patients.

item.title: Epilepsy in paediatric neurofibromatosis type 1: clinical features and associated factors in a single-centere cohort.
item.description:
European journal of pediatrics
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is associated with an increased risk of epilepsy, but the clinical spectrum and associated factors of epilepsy in paediatric NF1 remain incompletely characterized. We aimed to describe frequency and features of epilepsy in paediatric NF1 and to compare the characteristics of NF1 patients with and without epilepsy. We retrospectively reviewed 253 paediatric NF1 patients followed up between January 2020 and December 2025. Demographic, clinical, electroencephalographic, and radiological data were collected. Categorical comparisons between patients with and without epilepsy were performed using χ2 or Fisher's exact tests. Of 253 patients (53.8% female; median age 12.3 years), 12 (4.74%) had epilepsy. Median age at epilepsy onset was 3.2 years (IQR 2.4-7.0). Seizure semiology was focal in 7 (58.3%) and generalized in 5 (41.7%). EEG reports were available in 10 patients: normal in 4, focal discharges in 4, and multifocal discharges in 2; no patient had generalized spike-and-wave discharges. Four (33.3%) had drug-resistant epilepsy; median number of antiseizure medications was 1, median seizure-free duration was 44 months. Compared with patients without epilepsy, those with epilepsy had significantly higher rates of moyamoya syndrome (25.0% vs 0.4%, p < 0.001), autism spectrum disorder (16.7% vs 0%, p = 0.002), learning difficulties (58.3% vs 14.5%, p < 0.001), and overall neurodevelopmental comorbidity (83.3% vs 29.0%, p < 0.001). No significant differences were found in the frequencies of neurofibromatosis bright objects (NBOs), optic pathway gliomas, or low-grade gliomas. Conclusions In our cohort, epilepsy occurred in 4.74% of patients. Most had favorable seizure outcomes. Epilepsy was associated with cerebrovascular anomalies and neurodevelopmental comorbidities but not with NBOs or intracranial tumours. These findings suggest that children with NF1 and cerebrovascular abnormalities may warrant particular vigilance for seizures, while those with epilepsy should undergo systematic neurodevelopmental assessment. What is known • Epilepsy affects 4-14% of patients with NF1, is usually mild, but its determinants remain poorly defined. • Neurofibromatosis bright objects show no consistent association with epilepsy. What is new • In 253 children, epilepsy (4.74%) was associated with moyamoya syndrome and neurodevelopmental comorbidity. • Optic pathway gliomas, low-grade gliomas and bright objects did not predict epilepsy.

item.title: Sensorimotor cortex activity during cued gait differs in Parkinson’s freezers and non-freezers
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Gait impairments are a major contributor to disability in patients with Parkinson’s disease despite dopaminergic and neuromodulation therapies. External cues (e.g., visual targets, rhythmic auditory sounds) are commonly used to improve gait quality and reduce freezing of gait (FOG), yet their effectiveness varies across patients and contexts. Improved understanding of the neural mechanisms of cueing benefits is essential to personalize rehabilitation strategies and improve outcomes. We use mobile electroencephalography (EEG) to test the hypothesis that cues improve gait through engagement of voluntary motor control mechanisms to compensate for impaired gait automaticity. In addition, we investigate whether this mechanism is related to cueing benefits or freezing status. Eighteen PD patients with a history of freezing (PD-F), 21 patients without freezing (PD-NF) and 19 age-matched healthy controls (HC) walked overground under three conditions: normal walking, synchronizing to auditory cues, and stepping over visual cues. Stride-locked beta band (13–30 Hz) power dynamics in sensorimotor cortex were used to measure cortical control of stepping. Spatiotemporal gait parameters improved with cues in all groups. However, PD-F had smaller cue-related gains in speed and stride length when compared with PD-NF for both cue types, and did not improve gait speed with visual cues. EEG revealed greater contralateral sensorimotor cortex swing-phase beta suppression in PD-F than PD-NF patients, with visual cues eliciting the most robust response. In contrast, beta suppression with cues was less pronounced in PD-NF and HC, despite greater behavioral gains. In addition, engagement of sensorimotor cortex during visual cueing was associated with divergent gait effects across PD subgroups: In PD-NF greater beta suppression was associated with less gait improvement, whereas in PD-F the opposite was observed. These findings suggest distinct sensorimotor control mechanisms for cue utilization in PD-F and PD-NF, and indicate that engagement of voluntary motor control circuits may underlie cueing benefits primarily in PD-F.

item.title: The Paradoxical Effect of Levetiracetam: A Case of Nonconvulsive Status Epilepticus Following Stereoelectroencephalography Implantation.
item.description:
Clinical EEG and neuroscience
The paradoxical effect of levetiracetam (LEV) refers to the paradoxical aggravation of epileptic seizures during clinical application. In this case, we report for the first time a patient with MRI-negative drug-resistant frontal lobe epilepsy who developed nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) following LEV dose escalation, as documented by stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG). The SEEG findings suggested that paradoxical activation of mesial temporal structures may be involved in the occurrence of LEV-induced paradoxical effects.

item.title: Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Science advances
Schizophrenia disrupts both how people perceive the world and how they express and act on their thoughts, yet these symptoms are usually studied separately. Using magnetoencephalography during multisensory and motor tasks, we tested whether reduced event-related beta-band (15 to 30 hertz) modulation, a signal implicated in predictive control, provides a candidate neural marker across these domains. Compared to healthy individuals, patients showed diminished beta changes during sensory processing and movement completion, suggesting reduced flexibility in updating internal models. This neural pattern covaried with audiovisual simultaneity-judgment behavior, disorganized natural speech, and greater clinical severity. These findings suggest that distributed beta modulation may serve as a candidate cross-domain marker associated with perceptual, motor, and language disturbances in schizophrenia, motivating future studies that directly test predictive updating mechanisms.

item.title: EEG Edge-Centric Dynamics Reveal Distinct Post-Stroke Somatosensory Network Responses to Vibratory and Electrical Stimulation.
item.description:
IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
Stroke-induced somatosensory deficits disrupt sensorimotor integration (SMI) and limit motor recovery, yet the immediate network-level effects of different somatosensory interventions remain unclear, hindering patient-specific rehabilitation planning. We propose an informatics framework based on edge-centric dynamic connectivity (ECDC) to characterize transient, whole-brain EEG network responses to sensory-level focal vibratory stimulation (FVS) and neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES). We analyzed EEG recordings from 15 chronic stroke participants and 15 healthy controls during forearm stimulation and quantified temporal network dynamics, spectral network organization, and interhemispheric interactions from instantaneous overlapping functional networks. Compared with NMES, FVS in stroke participants induced a distinct neurophysiological profile, including (i) shorter global theta-network latency, suggesting faster attentional engagement; (ii) higher contralesional alpha network diversity, indicating enhanced somatosensory recruitment; and (iii) reduced theta-alpha phase-amplitude coupling, reflecting decoupled interhemispheric interactions that may support adaptive reorganization. These findings provide interpretable network signatures for differentiating stimulation-specific brain responses and suggest a data driven route toward personalized SMI rehabilitation.

item.title: ADHD symptom positivity and its association with medication adherence and psychiatric burden in adults with epilepsy.
item.description:
Epilepsy & behavior : E&B
Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms are increasingly recognized in adults with epilepsy (AwE) and may contribute to psychiatric burden, seizure-related outcomes, and treatment adherence. We therefore investigated the frequency of ADHD symptom positivity and its associations with medication adherence, psychiatric symptoms, seizure burden, and neurophysiological findings. Methods This cross-sectional study included 100 AwE and 94 healthy controls. ADHD symptoms were assessed using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1). Anxiety and depressive symptoms were evaluated using the Beck Anxiety Inventory and Beck Depression Inventory, respectively. Medication adherence was assessed using the Morisky Medication Adherence Scale (MMAS-8). Participants were classifiedas ASRS-positive or ASRS-negative according to the six-item ASRS Part A screener. Clinical, psychiatric, electroencephalographic, and magnetic resonance imaging findings were compared between groups. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors independently associated with ADHD-symptom-positivity. Results ADHD-symptom-positivity was significantly more frequent in AwE than in healthy controls (50.0% vs. 25.5%, p = 0.001). Within the epilepsy cohort, ASRS-positive participants demonstrated lower medication adherence (p = 0.010), higher rates of poor adherence (70.0% vs. 48.0%, p = 0.042), higher anxiety (p = 0.002), and depression scores (p < 0.001). Clinically significant anxiety and depression were also more common among ASRS-positive participants (p = 0.027 and p < 0.001, respectively). In multivariable analysis, depression score was independently associated with ADHD-symptom-positivity (OR = 1.147, 95% CI 1.039-1.267, p = 0.007). Conclusions ADHD-symptom-positivity is common in AwE and is associated with poorer medication adherence in the between-group analysis, but this association did not remain statistically significant after multivariable adjustment, while greater psychiatric symptom burden was observed. Routine screening for ADHD-related symptoms may facilitate identification of adults with epilepsy at increased riskfor adverse clinical outcomes and support more comprehensive epilepsy care.

item.title: The mediating effect of circulating C-reactive protein on the association between depression and brain cortical dysconnectivity.
item.description:
Psychiatry research. Neuroimaging
Chronic low grade systemic inflammation is associated in the pathophysiology of major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the specific cortical structural connectivity changes associated with peripheral inflammation in MDD remains poorly understood. In this case-control study, 113 MDD patients and 107 healthy controls underwent 3T MRI and measurement of high sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP). Fiber connectivity density (FiCD) mapping, a data driven whole-cortex pipeline combining cortical surface reconstruction with diffusion tractography, was used to examine depression and CRP interaction effects on cortical connectivity. A subgroup of MDD patients completed a six-week antidepressant follow-up with repeat MRI. A significant interaction between depression and CRP was identified in the left rostral middle frontal cortex (LRMF). FiCD in the LRMF was significantly lower in MDD patients than controls and negatively correlated with CRP in patients but not controls. Following six weeks of antidepressant treatment, FiCD in LRMF increased significantly, and this increase was negatively correlated with baseline. Peripheral inflammation is possibly associated with disrupted cortical connectivity in MDD and disturbs the brain structural recovery process during antidepressant treatment. The left rostral middle frontal cortex possibly serves as an important target.

item.title: Characterizing post-stroke changes in brain microstructure using the mean apparent propagator model.
item.description:
NeuroImage. Clinical
This study investigated regional and whole-brain microstructural alterations following stroke using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and Mean Apparent Propagator MRI (MAP-MRI). Multi-shell diffusion and T1-weighted MRI data were analyzed from participants with chronic stroke and healthy controls. DTI-derived fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD), and MAP-MRI-derived return-to-origin (RTOP), return-to-axis (RTAP), and return-to-plane (RTPP) probabilities were quantified across 13 predefined regions in native diffusion space. Regional group differences were assessed using participant-level median values with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) correction across all 65 ROI × diffusion-metric comparisons and age- and sex-adjusted sensitivity analyses. Complementary lesion-relative whole-brain analyses used nonparametric permutation testing with threshold-free cluster enhancement and family-wise error correction. MAP-MRI demonstrated widespread regional abnormalities, with significant group differences in 11 of 13 regions for RTOP, 12 of 13 for RTAP, and 10 of 13 for RTPP, compared with 8 of 13 for FA and all 13 regions for MD. After adjustment for age and sex, significant differences remained in 11, 10, and 9 regions for RTOP, RTAP, and RTPP, respectively, compared with 6 for FA and all 13 for MD. Whole-brain analyses demonstrated significant corrected abnormalities across all five diffusion metrics, with RTOP and RTAP showing the most spatially extensive Control > Stroke effects, followed by RTPP and FA, whereas MD showed extensive effects in the opposite, Stroke > Control direction. Regional discrimination varied by anatomical region and metric, without a uniform advantage of MAP-MRI over DTI. Exploratory diffusion-function analyses identified several nominal associations, but none survived correction across all comparisons. These findings demonstrate complementary, region- and metric-specific sensitivity of MAP-MRI and DTI to chronic stroke-related microstructural abnormalities. MAP-MRI identified distributed abnormalities across regional and whole-brain analyses, while MD remained highly sensitive to widespread tissue differences. The differing spatial distributions and regional discriminative performance of MAP-MRI and DTI suggest that these approaches capture partially distinct features of the post-stroke diffusion environment. Together, these findings support their complementary use for characterizing distributed microstructural abnormalities following chronic stroke.

item.title: Treatment-associated structural connectome reorganization following high-frequency rTMS in major depressive disorder: A low- and high-order connectivity study.
item.description:
Journal of psychiatric research
