Background High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is an established treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), but associated changes in structural-connectome topology remains unclear. Specifically, higher-order structural connectivity (HOSC), defined by similarities between regional structural connectivity profiles, may provide information beyond direct low-order structural connectivity (LOSC). Methods Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data were acquired from 23 patients with MDD before and after 10-Hz rTMS and from 30 matched healthy controls (HCs). LOSC networks were constructed based on deterministic tractography, whereas HOSC networks were derived from similarities between regional LOSC profiles. Graph-theoretical analysis and network-based statistics were employed to characterize topological and subnetwork differences. Results Depressive symptoms decreased significantly after treatment. Global LOSC topology remained stable, whereas HOSC showed case-control differences in network segregation and post-treatment differences in small-world organization relative to HCs. Network-based analysis revealed focal strengthening of a left insula-hippocampal-inferior temporal component in LOSC and distributed HOSC variation involving cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuitry, particularly the thalamus and caudate. Nodal analyses further identified treatment-associated centrality changes involving the thalamus and hippocampus. Conclusion High-frequency rTMS treatment was associated with coordinated structural-connectome variation across low- and high-order network organization in MDD. These findings should be interpreted as treatment-associated changes rather than effects attributable specifically to rTMS and suggest that HOSC may provide a complementary representation of network variation accompanying clinical improvement.

item.title: Profiles of Chronic Pain and Cognitive Concerns: A Cluster Analysis Among Older Adults Enrolled in a Mind-body Activity Intervention.
item.description:
The journal of pain
Chronic pain and cognitive concerns are highly comorbid, particularly among older adults, though the specific severity and symptom overlap may vary across individuals. We aimed to characterize distinct profiles of individuals with chronic pain and subjective cognitive concerns (concern of persistent cognitive decline, with or without objective cognitive deficits) and compare demographic/psychosocial variables between subgroups. We analyzed baseline data from an ongoing randomized controlled trial comparing a mind-body activity intervention to a health education control. As part of the larger study, older adults with chronic musculoskeletal pain and subjective cognitive concerns completed measures of pain severity (NRS), pain interference (PROMIS), and subjective (ECog-12) and objective cognitive dysfunction (RBANS). Participants also completed measures of mental health symptoms (anxiety, depression), general psychosocial factors (loneliness, mindfulness, self-compassion, coping skills), and pain-specific psychological factors (pain catastrophizing, kinesiophobia, pain self-efficacy). An exploratory hierarchical cluster analysis examined unique symptom profiles among participants with complete data (n=251) on the four pain/cognitive dysfunction variables, and multivariate logistic regression models examined cluster membership by demographic and psychosocial variables. We identified a three-cluster solution: (1) lowest symptom burden (n=101); (2) mixed symptom burden (n=93); and (3) highest symptom burden (n=57). Several demographic, mental health, and psychosocial factors significantly distinguished between subgroup membership. Results elucidate the heterogeneity in clinical presentations within these two overlapping conditions and suggest specific potential risk factors for experiencing greater symptom burden. Findings overall represent an important first step in identifying which older adults may benefit most from interventions for co-occurring chronic pain and cognitive concerns. PERSPECTIVE: This article characterizes distinct profiles of older adults with chronic pain and cognitive concerns and suggests potential risk factors for experiencing greater symptom burden. Findings can help inform which older adults are most likely to benefit from interventions targeting co-occurring chronic pain and cognitive concerns.

item.title: EEG-VTSFN: An enhanced approach for differentiating between unipolar and bipolar mood disorders.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Accurate differentiation between Bipolar Disorder (BD) and Unipolar Depression (UD) is a significant clinical challenge due to overlapping manifestations and a lack of objective biomarkers. While EEG offers high temporal resolution, its psychiatric utility for diagnostic differentiation remains limited. To address this, we propose the Variational Autoencoder (VAE)-based Time-Space Fusion Network (VTSFN). VTSFN transforms complex EEG signals into latent-space representations to mitigate noise and construct stable latent co-activation patterns. By integrating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and attention mechanisms, the model captures temporal dynamics to identify discriminative patterns. Our results demonstrate that VTSFN achieved the highest accuracy and AUC point estimates among the evaluated models, with a test-set accuracy of 79.3% (95% CI, 65.5%-93.1%) and an AUC of 82.7% (95% CI, 63.2%-98.5%), without significant paired AUC differences at p < 0.01. Validation in a diagnostic-switch (tBD) cohort (n = 22) identified 17/22 converters (sensitivity, 77.3%; 95% CI, 59.1%-90.9%), requiring further longitudinal validation. Exploratory feature analysis revealed that, compared with UD patients, BD and tBD patients exhibited weaker latent co-activation in right parieto-temporal and temporo-occipital regions, alongside stronger latent co-activation in left frontal-right parietal and temporal regions. These model-derived channel similarity patterns require independent validation.

item.title: Thalamocortical dysconnectivity shapes cortical hierarchy disruption across illness durations in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Schizophrenia is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of circuit-level dysfunction. However, how thalamocortical abnormalities differ across cohorts with varying illness durations and relate to large-scale cortical hierarchical organization remains unclear. Methods We analyzed resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 1,223 patients with schizophrenia and 1,224 matched healthy controls across 12 datasets. The datasets were grouped as early-, middle-, and late-stage cohorts. Connectivity gradient mapping was applied to characterize thalamocortical organization, and computational modeling evaluated simulated hierarchical changes after modifying thalamic-salience connectivity. Results We identified a schizophrenia-relevant sensorimotor-salience-association axis that captures systematic differences in thalamocortical abnormality profiles across the stage cohorts. Along this axis, case-control effects in association regions were positive in the early-stage cohort but negative in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, whereas sensorimotor regions showed the converse pattern. This cross-cohort pattern was accompanied by reduced cortical hierarchical separation in cohorts with longer illness duration. In contrast, salience-related thalamic regions showed negative case-control effects in all three stage cohorts, with larger effect sizes in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, and these alterations were associated with clinical symptoms. Computational modification of thalamic-salience connectivity increased simulated cortical hierarchical differentiation, particularly in the middle-stage cohort. Conclusions These findings indicate that thalamocortical dysconnectivity, centered on disrupted thalamic-salience interactions, is associated with systematic differences in cortical hierarchical organization across cohorts. The cross-cohort pattern of salience-related abnormalities highlights thalamic-salience coupling as a circuit-level link to cortical hierarchical differentiation and a candidate for future mechanistic and interventional investigation.

item.title: Multi-Parametric Phase-Cycled Balanced Steady-State Free Precession Brain Tissue Characterization in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis.
item.description:
Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
Background Time-efficient phase-cycled balanced steady-state free precession (pc-bSSFP) imaging is a novel microstructure- and myelin-sensitive approach for multi-parametric brain tissue characterization not yet evaluated in demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS). Purpose To evaluate quantitative relaxometry metrics in white matter (WM) and gray matter (GM) of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) and healthy control (HC) cohorts using a multi-parametric pc-bSSFP framework. Study type Prospective and retrospective, observational. Population Twenty RRMS patients (34.5 ± 5.9 years, female 15/20) and 10 HC subjects (33.4 ± 6.9 years, female 5/10). Field strength/sequence 3 T; T1 -weighted magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo, T2 -weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, pc-bSSFP, B1 + mapping, single-shot spin-echo echo-planar-imaging diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Assessment R1 , R2 , and the bSSFP asymmetry index (AI) were compared between RRMS and HC across selected WM and GM regions of interest (ROIs). DTI-derived fiber-to-field angle, number of fiber orientations, and fractional anisotropy were used for parameter anisotropy analysis. Statistical tests Linear mixed-effects models tested group, ROI, and group-by-ROI effects for each metric. Anisotropy differences between cohorts were assessed with two-sided t-tests. ROI and anisotropy tests employed false discovery rate correction with significance set at pcorr < 0.05. Results Significant group, ROI, and group-by-ROI effects were found for R1 (β = -0.16) and R2 (β = -2.84). The ROI effect was significant for AI while the group (p = 0.450) and group-by-ROI (p = 0.747) effects were non-significant. Age and sex covariates did not reach significance (Age: p = [0.563, 0.705, 0.591], Gender: p = [0.839, 0.822, 0.179], for [R1 , R2 , AI]). Fourteen of 16 ROIs showed significantly lower R1 and R2 (d = -4.25 to -0.85) in RRMS than HC. All ROIs remained non-significant for AI. R2 (pcorr ≥ 0.055) and AI (pcorr ≥ 0.108) anisotropy comparison between RRMS and HC groups did not reach significance. Data conclusion Phase-cycled bSSFP relaxometry showed WM-predominant differences in RRMS, with additional whole-brain assessment including gray matter. Evidence level 2. Technical efficacy Stage 1.

item.title: Multimodal Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Relapse in Major Depressive Disorder.
item.description:
JAMA psychiatry
Importance Early identification of patients at high risk of relapse is key to personalized preventive strategies in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, current predictive models do not adequately account for the multimodal factors contributing to MDD relapse and fail to provide clinically meaningful predictions. Objective To predict relapse within 2 years in patients with MDD by using a comprehensive machine learning pipeline that integrates an unprecedented set of multimodal data. Design, setting, and participants This naturalistic longitudinal prognostic study used data from the Marburg-Münster Affective Disorders Cohort Study, with baseline assessments collected from October 2014 to May 2019 and follow-up approximately 2 years later, between October 2016 and June 2021. Data analysis was conducted between July 2024 and June 2026. The study was performed at 2 sites in Germany (Marburg and Münster), with participants recruited from psychiatric inpatient and outpatient departments and the general population. Patients meeting diagnostic criteria for current or lifetime MDD without history of neurological or severe somatic conditions were included. Exposure Natural course of illness in patients with MDD. Main outcomes and measures Balanced accuracy (BACC) for binary prediction of relapse vs no relapse during 2-year follow-up served as the primary outcome. Baseline features comprised 9 modalities including clinical and psychometric data, 4 structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging modalities, genetics, neurocognition, blood markers, and gut microbiome. Results A total of 564 patients with a current or lifetime MDD diagnosis were included (367 female [65.1%]; mean [SD] age, 37.34 [13.38] years). A total of 270 patients relapsed during the 2-year follow-up, while 294 did not. Mean (SD) BACC for the prediction of relapse ranged from 47.21% (5.85%) to 64.43% (6.63%). The best-performing model was solely based on few clinical relapse risk factors, while multimodal data integration did not improve performance. Conclusions and relevance In this prognostic study, the models achieved moderate accuracy, yet the results suggest limited scope for guiding individual-level clinical decision-making. Predictive performance was largely driven by established clinical risk factors, indicating limited incremental value of multimodal measures when assessed at a single time point. Future advances may instead benefit from dynamic modeling approaches that more closely align temporally evolving multimodal markers with longitudinal clinical outcomes.

item.title: REM Sleep Iota Oscillations Across the Lifespan
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Iota oscillations are a newly discovered marker of wakefulness and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. So far, iota in REM sleep has only been reported in the surface electroencephalography (EEG) of a small sample of young adults and in intracranial recordings of epileptic patients. Here, we investigated the presence of these oscillations in a large dataset (N=937) of high-density sleep EEG recordings from individuals 7 to 70 years old. We found that iota spectral peaks during REM sleep were between 25 and 40 Hz, slightly faster than in wake (25-35 Hz). Iota power was significantly associated with REM sleep architecture, increasing with both REM duration and across progressive sleep cycles. Iota peaks were observed in individuals of all ages, although the prevalence decreased gradually with age, from 88% in children to 44% in older adults. Most iota spectral peak properties (frequency, amplitude, timing, topography) likewise shifted with age. The most striking effect, however, was in bandwidth, such that children had narrow iota peaks, older adults had broad iota peaks, and 20-30 year olds could have either. It remains unclear whether narrowband and broadband iota are functionally equivalent. On shorter time scales (< 1 year), iota properties remained stable across measurements. Analyses of a separate dataset of monozygotic and dizygotic twins revealed high heritability of all iota peak properties except bandwidth. Overall, these results establish iota as a genetically determined trait-like marker of REM sleep with unique age-related changes. Iota oscillations open new avenues to investigate the interaction between sleep, genetics, development, and aging.

item.title: Comparing re-referencing methods for human intracranial EEG
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) involves the implantation of depth electrodes in the brain to monitor epileptic seizures for surgical feasibility. As the electrodes advance into deeper limbic structures, the macro contacts distributed along the shaft record electrical activity from more lateral sites, while a bundled array of microwires simultaneously captures highly localised signals from the tip of the electrode. In a clinical setting these electrical signals are recorded relative to a reference signal, which may be sub-optimal for subsequent analyses that are unrelated to clinical objectives. Therefore, a secondary re-referencing operation is often undertaken to transform the signal in relation to a specific hypothesis. Despite a recent surge in SEEG studies, comparative studies on the much-understudied issue of re-referencing are sparse. Here, we analyse data collected from 16 human patients during an episodic memory task and comparatively apply a range of re-referencing methods to both macro contact and micro-wire data. We find that the choice of method changes the proportion of trials that survive artefact rejection, low frequency power, and the aperiodic background against which that power is read. In the hippocampal recordings, however, no method differed from any other in the size of a memory effect in power or spike–field coherence. This early transformative decision therefore bears on how the signal is described. We found no evidence that it changes the detectability of the behavioural effects tested here, and no method reversed the direction of a memory effect.

item.title: Neurodegeneration epicenters: Distinct network mechanisms of dopaminergic treatment in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Neural regeneration research
Abstract Parkinson's disease exhibits heterogeneous spatiotemporal patterns of neurodegeneration. Dopaminergic therapy improves motor symptoms by modulating brain function in affected regions, yet whether the neural mechanisms through which dopaminergic therapy exerts its effects are linked to this heterogeneity of neurodegeneration remains unclear. A connectivity-based epicenter framework combined with spectral dynamic causal modeling was applied to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 160 drug-naïve Parkinson's disease patients and 174 healthy controls to identify subtype-specific degenerative epicenters and characterize directional interactions among affected regions. Ninety-seven patients additionally underwent an acute levodopa challenge to evaluate how dopaminergic modulation influences these interactions and relates to symptom improvements. Two distinct Parkinson's disease subtypes were identified: subtype 1 was characterized by degenerative epicenters predominantly located in subcortical and cerebellar regions, whereas subtype 2 exhibited epicenters primarily involving cortical regions. Both subtypes exhibited widespread dysregulation of directional interactions among epicenter regions relative to healthy controls. Levodopa treatment partially reversed these network abnormalities in a manner specific to each subtype, notably within cerebellar vermis in subtype 1 and frontal cortex in subtype 2. Symptom improvements were linked to distinct network interactions: in subtype 1, tremor correlated with the thalamus, midbrain nuclei, and cerebellar vermis, whereas bradykinesia primarily involved the cerebellar vermis; in subtype 2, rigidity improvements mapped to frontal cortex and limbic regions, and bradykinesia to limbic regions. These findings suggest that Parkinson's disease involves distinct epicenter networks in each subtype, with widespread directional dysregulation contributing to symptom diversity in patients. Levodopa treatment selectively modulates these network interactions, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying treatment heterogeneity and guiding precision-targeted therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Predictive EEG Signatures of Alzheimer's Disease: A Cross-Validated, Cross-Method Analysis Using ANCOVA Filtering and Sparse Logistic Regression
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) changes how the brain’s electrical activity behaves, and these changes can, in principle, be picked up directly from a resting-state EEG recording without any invasive testing. This study asks a much narrower question: does a small subset of four EEG-derived measurement families, namely signal complexity, spectral power, functional connectivity and network topology, reliably separate individuals with AD from Healthy Controls (HC), and does that separation hold up under strict, leakage-free testing? Using a public dataset of 36 AD and 29 HC subjects, candidate features were selected through permutation-based ANCOVA with false discovery rate correction, controlling for age and gender, and each selected feature was then re-checked using a complementary method (Mann-Whitney U with FDR correction, plus network-based statistics for connectivity), applied to the same subjects, to confirm the finding wasn’t an artifact of the first method’s particular assumptions. Agreement between the two methods was strong for signal complexity (Jaccard = 0.85) and spectral power (Jaccard = 0.87), essentially perfect for two of the four network measures (Jaccard = 1.00), and weaker for connectivity (Jaccard = 0.60, assessed at the level of frequency bands). A sparse logistic regression classifier was then trained using 5-fold cross-validation in which feature selection was independently repeated inside each fold, a design specifically intended to stop information from test subjects leaking into which features get chosen. This classifier reached 78.5% ± 5.8% accuracy at discriminating AD from HC (sensitivity 0.803 ± 0.116, specificity 0.753 ± 0.100, AUC 0.808 ± 0.134). A single spectral power feature was among the two features retained in three of the five folds, more than any other individual feature. Taken together, the results point to a real but modest EEG signature of AD in this dataset, identified using a validation design built specifically so that reported accuracy reflects genuine generalization rather than an artifact of how the features were selected.

item.title: Molecularly distinct neurodegeneration shapes the DOPA-dependent dynamic of large-scale brain connectomics in GBA-associated Parkinson’s disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract GBA1-associated Parkinson’s disease (GBA1-PD) is a biologically distinct synucleinopathy associated with glucocerebrosidase deficiency, lysosomal dysfunction, and more extensive cortical neurodegeneration. How these molecular abnormalities shape large-scale cortical network dynamics in vivo remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize resting-state EEG functional connectivity and network topology in GBA1-PD and to determine whether GBA1-related molecular pathology is associated with a distinct oscillatory connectome signature and its modulation by dopaminergic treatment. We recorded resting-state EEG in 22 patients with PD (GBA1-PD = 7; LRRK2-PD = 5; sporadic PD = 10) together with 14 age-matched healthy controls. EEG was acquired in OFF and ON dopaminergic states. Functional connectivity was estimated using imaginary coherence (ImCoh) and phase-locking value (PLV) across canonical frequency bands, while network organization was quantified using the graph-theoretical clustering coefficient. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess therapy- and subtype-specific effects. GBA1-PD exhibited a selective increase in gamma-band clustering coefficient in the ON condition (p = 0.044), which was not observed in LRRK2 or sporadic PD. PLV-based analyses highlighted opposite clustering changes in GBA1 and LRRK2 patients. ImCoh analyses further revealed different therapy-related connectivity changes in genetic and sporadic PD across all frequency bands (all p ≤ 0.0035). Compared with healthy controls, PD was associated with widespread disruption of cortico-cortical connectivity. All significant effects were abolished in surrogate-data analyses, supporting their physiological specificity. Resting-state EEG connectomics may reveal genotype-specific network alterations in GBA1-PD and their modulation by dopaminergic treatment, supporting a relationship between genetic background and large-scale brain network dynamics.

item.title: ADHDeepNet: An Explainable Framework for EEG-Based ADHD Detection From Raw Signals.
item.description:
Biomedical physics & engineering express
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common brain disorder in children that can persist into adulthood, affecting social, academic, and career life. Early diagnosis is crucial for managing these impacts on patients and the healthcare system but is often labor-intensive and time-consuming. This paper presents a novel method to improve ADHD diagnosis precision and timeliness by leveraging Deep Learning (DL) approaches and electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. We introduce ADHDeepNet, a deep learning model that utilizes comprehensive temporal-spatial characterization, attention modules, and explainability techniques optimized for EEG signals. ADHDeepNet integrates feature extraction and refinement processes to enhance ADHD diagnosis. The model was trained and validated on a dataset of 121 participants (61 ADHD, 60 Healthy Controls), employing nested cross-validation for robust performance. The proposed two-stage methodology uses a 10-fold cross-subject validation strategy. Initially, each iteration optimizes the model's hyper-parameters with inner 2-fold cross-validation. Then, Additive Gaussian Noise (AGN) with various standard deviations and magnification levels is applied for data augmentation. ADHDeepNet achieved 100% sensitivity and 99.17% accuracy in classifying ADHD/HC subjects. To clarify model explainability and identify key brain regions and frequency bands for ADHD diagnosis, we analyzed the learned weights and activation patterns of the model's primary layers. Additionally, t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) visualized high-dimensional data, aiding in interpreting the model's decisions. This study highlights the potential of deep learning and EEG in enhancing ADHD diagnosis accuracy and efficiency.
